title: How Jumping Spiders Sleep - Nautilus
gist: A PNAS study led by German biologists examined sleep in Australian jumping spiders (Portia fimbriata) using a novel approach, finding sleep cycles remarkably like humans', including REM-like phases. Invertebrate sleep remains far less understood than human sleep.

insights.claim: Sleep research has concentrated on humans, and far less is known about invertebrate sleep patterns despite invertebrates also needing sleep.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Points to an under-researched scientific frontier.
insights.locator: Myriad studies focus on human sleep

insights.claim: A study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, led by biologists in Germany with colleagues from Australia and Italy, examined sleep in Australian jumping spiders (Portia fimbriata).
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
entities: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
insights.so_what: Cross-national basic research output; limited direct investment relevance.

insights.claim: Because an electroencephalogram is impractical on a spider the length of a rice grain, the researchers had to devise a new approach to measuring spider sleep.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Shows methodological innovation in measuring tiny-organism physiology.
insights.quote: It’s obviously tough to conduct an electroencephalogram on a spider the length of a rice grain.

insights.claim: Jumping spiders sleep in cycles remarkably like humans, including wakefulness and REM-like phases.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Suggests sleep architecture is evolutionarily widespread, relevant to sleep-biology research.
insights.quote: Remarkably like us with cycles of wakefulness and REM

insights.claim: These arachnids are typically active by day and sleep at night with legs pulled in, a posture that camouflages them against foliage or rocks.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese

top_entities: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
